19:T2f32,### Introduction
Axeline "Queen Agnes" Elizabeth Salomon (c. 1858 – after 1888) was a legendary labor leader and resistance fighter in the Danish West Indies (modern-day U.S. Virgin Islands). She rose to historical prominence as one of the "Four Queens" who led the historic 1878 labor rebellion on the island of St. Croix, an event popularly known as the "Fireburn" [1]. Alongside [Queen Mary](/profiles/queen-mary) (Mary Thomas), [Queen Mathilda](/profiles/queen-mathilda) (Mathilda McBean), and Susana "Bottom Belly" Abramsen, Queen Agnes organized and mobilized plantation laborers to rise up against the oppressive, semi-feudal labor contracts imposed by Danish colonial authorities [2]. Her actions during the revolt, particularly at the Carlton Plantation, and her subsequent imprisonment in Denmark and St. Croix, made her a symbol of Caribbean working-class resistance, gendered leadership, and the struggle for human dignity.

![The Three Queens Fountain monument in Charlotte Amalie, St. Thomas, featuring Queen Mary, Queen Agnes, and Queen Mathilda](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4c/ThreeQueensSTT.jpg)

### Socio-Economic Context: Post-Emancipation Peonage
To understand the rise of Queen Agnes, one must examine the socio-economic conditions of St. Croix in the mid-to-late nineteenth century. In 1848, Governor Peter von Scholten officially emancipated the enslaved population of the Danish West Indies in the face of a massive, organized uprising of enslaved workers. However, the plantocracy and the Danish colonial government quickly moved to subvert this newly won freedom. In 1849, the colonial administration enacted the Labor Act (Arbejdsregulativet), which designed a system of debt peonage that bound formerly enslaved workers to their plantations in conditions that closely mirrored slavery [3].

Under this act, laborers were forced to sign annual contracts. They were classified as "first-class," "second-class," or "third-class" workers, receiving extremely low wages. They were required to work long, grueling hours—typically from sunrise to sunset—and were forbidden from leaving their plantations without written permission from their employers. The only day of the year when workers were permitted to terminate their contracts, seek new employers, or leave their estates was October 1st, which became known as "Contract Day" or "Quarter Day" [3].

By 1878, thirty years after emancipation, the laborers’ frustration reached a boiling point. Wages had stagnated or decreased, inflation had driven up the cost of basic goods, and the island had suffered from droughts and crop failures. Laborers realized that despite their legal freedom, they were trapped in a cycle of poverty and exploitation with no upward mobility.

### Early Life and Identity of Axeline Salomon
Axeline Elizabeth Salomon, who was commonly known by her middle name, Agnes, was born on St. Croix around 1858. Unlike the wealthy colonial administrators who kept detailed journals, the lives of Black working-class women like Agnes were rarely recorded in detail unless they ran afoul of the colonial legal system. Consequently, much of what historians know about Agnes’s early life comes from the police records, census data, and interrogation transcripts compiled after the 1878 uprising [4].

Agnes grew up on St. Croix, living and working within the network of sugar plantations that dominated the island’s economy. She was a member of the Moravian Church, a Protestant denomination that had a significant presence in the Danish West Indies and provided one of the few avenues of education and spiritual community for the Black population [4].

By the time of the rebellion in 1878, Agnes was an unmarried young woman of about twenty. She was already a mother of three children, a testament to the immense domestic and financial responsibilities she carried while laboring in the sugarcane fields [4]. Her daily life was defined by the double burden of agricultural labor under the hot Caribbean sun and the care of her young family, all within the constraints of the restrictive 1849 Labor Act.

### The Spark: October 1, 1878 (Contract Day)
On October 1, 1878, thousands of plantation workers from across St. Croix traveled to the port town of Frederiksted, which served as the commercial center for the island’s sugar trade. It was Contract Day, and the town was filled with laborers seeking to renew their agreements, change employers, or celebrate the brief moment of mobility granted by the law [2].

Tensions were high. Workers had hoped that the colonial government would announce the repeal of the Labor Act and a raise in the daily wage. When it became clear that no reforms were forthcoming, peaceful protests turned into angry demonstrations [3]. The situation escalated dramatically when a rumor spread through the crowd that a popular laborer named Henry Plum had been severely beaten by colonial police and had died in the local hospital.

Enraged by this apparent act of police brutality, the crowd descended upon the Frederiksted Fort (Fort Frederik), where the local police and military had barricaded themselves [2]. Lacking firearms, the workers used stones, sticks, and tools to attack the fort. When the military fired into the crowd, killing several protesters, the demonstration erupted into a full-scale insurrection [3]. The laborers, realizing they could not breach the fort’s stone walls, turned their anger toward the town itself, systematically setting fire to the commercial buildings and sugar warehouses.

### The Carlton Plantation Uprising and Agnes's Leadership
As the fires consumed Frederiksted, the rebellion spread outward into the rural plantation districts [2]. The workers organized themselves into groups, marching from estate to estate, dismantling machinery, and burning sugarcane fields and plantation houses. It was during this phase that Axeline Salomon emerged as a key strategist and leader, earning the title "Queen."

On the morning of Wednesday, October 2, 1878, Agnes was active at the Carlton Plantation, a large sugar estate located east of Frederiksted [5]. Carlton became the site of a violent clash. A group of Danish soldiers, sent to reinforce Frederiksted, had left a military cart at the plantation. A crowd of rebels, including Agnes, confronted the soldiers. In the ensuing struggle, two Danish soldiers were killed [5].

According to later testimonies from witnesses and co-defendants, Agnes played an active role in inciting the violence at Carlton [4]. She was described as carrying a lantern, using its flame to ignite the dry trash in the sugarcane fields and urging the crowd to confront the military. Interrogation records from the Commission of 1878 detail how Agnes spoke openly about the events, displaying a bold lack of fear that inspired her peers [4].

The rebellion raged for several days, destroying over fifty plantations and causing massive economic damage to the Danish colony [2]. The colonial governor deployed the military, supported by armed volunteers and sailors from foreign warships, to ruthlessly suppress the uprising. Over a hundred Black laborers were shot or executed, and hundreds more were arrested.

### The Colonial Crackdown and Trial
In the wake of the Fireburn, Danish authorities established a special military commission to investigate the rebellion and punish the leaders. Axeline Salomon was arrested and subjected to intense interrogation [4]. The trial records, preserved in the Danish National Archives, reveal the bias of the colonial judicial system, which was designed to protect the interests of the plantocracy and assert colonial dominance.

Despite these hostile conditions, Agnes and her co-defendants, including [Queen Mary](/profiles/queen-mary) and [Queen Mathilda](/profiles/queen-mathilda), remained defiant. On September 2, 1880, the commission sentenced Axeline Salomon to death for her role in the rebellion, specifically for her participation in the Carlton Plantation killings and arson [4]. The Supreme Court in Copenhagen confirmed the death sentence on May 23, 1881 [4].

However, executing three women who had become folk heroines threatened to spark further unrest. Seeking to defuse the situation, King Christian IX of Denmark commuted the death sentences of Agnes, Mary, and Mathilda to life imprisonment at hard labor [4].

### Exile and Imprisonment in Copenhagen
In July 1882, Agnes, Mary Thomas, and Mathilda McBean were placed aboard the Danish naval ship *Valdemar* and transported across the Atlantic to Denmark [2]. They were incarcerated in the Kvindefængslet på Christianshavn (the women's prison in Christianshavn, Copenhagen) [4].

The transition from the tropical climate of St. Croix to the cold, damp cells of Copenhagen was brutal. The women faced severe culture shock, freezing winters, and isolation. In prison, they were forced to perform hard labor, primarily sewing, knitting, and cleaning. Agnes’s prison records note that she arrived with almost no personal belongings, carrying only a single pair of earrings [4].

Despite their imprisonment, the "Queens of the Fireburn" captured the imagination of the Danish public. They were visited by journalists and artists, who were struck by their dignity and resilience. Their legacy of resistance was similar in spirit to other Caribbean slave rebellions, such as those led by [Bussa](/profiles/bussa) in Barbados, [Sam Sharpe](/profiles/sam-sharpe) in Jamaica, and [Tula](/profiles/tula) in Curaçao, showing a shared regional history of fighting against colonial bondage.

### Return to St. Croix
After serving several years in Denmark, the colonial administration decided to return the women to St. Croix. The cost of maintaining them in Copenhagen, combined with concerns about their health and growing public sympathy in Denmark, prompted their repatriation. In the late 1880s, Agnes, Mary, and Mathilda were sent back to St. Croix, where they were incarcerated at the Bassin Jailhouse in Christiansted to serve out the remainder of their sentences [2].

The traditional folk song of St. Croix commemorates their return and the memory of the jailhouse:

> *Queen Mary, oh where you gon' go burn?*
> *Queen Mary, oh where you gon' go burn?*
> *Don't ask me nothin' at all.*
> *Just give me the match and oil.*
> *Bassin Jailhouse, ah there the money there.* [1]

Agnes was eventually released from prison, though the exact date of her release and her life afterward remain obscured by history. She lived out her final years on the island she had fought to liberate, witnessing the gradual decline of the Danish colonial system.

### Legacy and Commemoration
Axeline "Queen Agnes" Salomon’s legacy is celebrated throughout the Virgin Islands. She represents the intersection of racial, class, and gender resistance in Caribbean history. In a society that sought to render Black working-class women invisible, Agnes forced her way into the historical record through her courage and leadership. Her struggle for labor rights echoed across the region, matching the later efforts of figures like [Clement Payne](/profiles/clement-payne) in Barbados and [David Hamilton Jackson](/profiles/hamilton-jackson) in St. Croix.

To honor her and her fellow leaders, the "Three Queens Fountain" was erected at Blackbeard’s Castle in Charlotte Amalie, St. Thomas. The monument features bronze statues of Queen Mary, Queen Agnes, and Queen Mathilda. Agnes is depicted holding a lantern, a tribute to her role in lighting the fires of resistance that swept across St. Croix in 1878 [2].

Every year on October 1st, Virgin Islanders celebrate Contract Day, reciting the names of the Queens and singing the folk songs that preserve their memory. Queen Agnes remains an enduring symbol of the fight for labor rights, freedom, and human dignity in the Caribbean.

![Frederiksted, St. Croix, where the Fireburn rebellion began on October 1, 1878](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5a/Frederiksted%2C_St_Croix_U.S._Virgin_Islands.JPG)a:["$","$L2","be3ca47d-e2d4-4e07-ba93-88d89d260458",{"href":"/profiles/queen-agnes","className":"group flex flex-col bg-white border border-navy/5 shadow-sm hover:shadow-xl transition-all duration-500","children":[["$","div",null,{"className":"relative aspect-[4/5] overflow-hidden","children":["$","img",null,{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e0/Three_Queens_Fountain_St_Thomas.jpg","alt":"Queen Agnes","className":"object-cover w-full h-full grayscale group-hover:grayscale-0 group-hover:scale-105 transition-all duration-700"}]}],["$","div",null,{"className":"p-6","children":[["$","h3",null,{"className":"font-serif text-xl text-navy mb-2 group-hover:text-gold transition-colors","children":"Queen Agnes"}],["$","p",null,{"className":"text-navy/60 text-xs line-clamp-3 leading-relaxed mb-4","children":"$19"}],"$L1a"]}]]}]
1b:T1c82,## Queen Mary: The Flame of Resistance in the Danish West Indies

### Introduction
Mary Thomas (c. 1848 – 1905), immortalized in history as "Queen Mary," is one of the most revered figures in the labor history of the Caribbean. A central leader of the 1878 St. Croix labor revolt known as the "Fireburn," her legacy is a testament to the enduring struggle for justice, dignity, and fair labor practices in the post-emancipation era. Emerging from the harsh realities of plantation life in the Danish West Indies (now the U.S. Virgin Islands), Queen Mary transformed from a laborer into a legendary symbol of resistance against colonial oppression and economic exploitation.

### The Post-Emancipation Reality
To understand the significance of Mary Thomas, one must understand the context of the Danish West Indies in the late 19th century. Although slavery was officially abolished in the colony in 1848—precipitated by a massive uprising led by figures like John Gottlieb (General Buddhoe)—the realities of freedom for the Black population were severely constrained. The colonial government instituted the Labor Act of 1849, a deeply oppressive system designed to maintain the plantation economy by binding workers to the land.

Under this system, workers were required to sign annual contracts on October 1st, known as "Contract Day." They were subjected to fixed, starvation-level wages, harsh working conditions, and severe restrictions on their mobility. The pass system effectively made it illegal for laborers to leave their plantations or seek better employment without the explicit permission of the estate owners. For thirty years, this system of indentured servitude bred deep resentment and a simmering anger among the laboring class.

### Early Life of Mary Thomas
Details about Mary Thomas's early life are relatively sparse, a common reality for working-class individuals and women of color in colonial records. It is believed she was born in Antigua around 1848, the very year slavery ended in the Danish territories. Sometime in the 1860s, she migrated to St. Croix, joining the workforce on the island's sugar plantations.

Before the events of 1878, records indicate she worked on various estates and had several children. She was known to be a woman of strong character, having been previously arrested for minor acts of defiance—a precursor to her future role as a revolutionary leader. Her life was defined by the grueling physical labor of the cane fields and the daily humiliations of a racially stratified and economically exploitative society.

> "Queen Mary, ah where you gon' go burn? / Queen Mary, ah where you gon' go burn? / Don't ask me nothin' t'all / Just give me the match and oil / Bassin Jailhouse, ah there the money dey."
> — Traditional Virgin Islands folk song commemorating the Fireburn.

### The Eruption of the Fireburn
The tension reached a breaking point on October 1, 1878. As laborers gathered in the town of Frederiksted for Contract Day, rumors circulated that the colonial authorities would deny their demands for higher wages and better living conditions. Furthermore, the workers' request to freely leave the island to seek better opportunities was vehemently opposed by the planters.

When their demands were flatly rejected, the accumulated anger of three decades erupted. The workers began to riot, targeting the symbols of their oppression: the sugar plantations and the colonial infrastructure. This uprising became known as the "Fireburn," the largest labor revolt in the history of the Danish colonial empire.

### The Three Queens
During the Fireburn, leadership naturally emerged from the ranks of the workers. Among the most prominent leaders were three women: Mary Thomas, Axeline "Agnes" Elizabeth Salomon, and Matilde McBean. The laborers bestowed the title of "Queen" upon them, a title that held deep cultural significance, rooted in African traditions and the social structures of Caribbean societies. The "Queens" were not only strategic leaders but also moral authorities who inspired the crowds and directed the course of the uprising.

Queen Mary, in particular, became the face of the rebellion. Armed with a cane knife and a torch, she was reportedly at the forefront of the demonstrations. The revolt lasted for several days, during which over 50 plantations—more than half the island's agricultural infrastructure—were set ablaze. The sky over St. Croix glowed red with the fires of resistance.

![I Am Queen Mary statue](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a2/I_Am_Queen_Mary.jpg)

### Suppression, Imprisonment, and Exile
The Danish colonial authorities responded with overwhelming military force. Troops were dispatched to crush the rebellion, resulting in the deaths of over a hundred laborers. Hundreds more were arrested in the brutal crackdown that followed.

Mary Thomas, along with Queen Agnes and Queen Matilda, was captured and brought before a military tribunal. Recognized as the instigators of the Fireburn, they were initially sentenced to death for their roles in the uprising. However, due to various political considerations and perhaps a fear of turning them into even greater martyrs, their sentences were commuted to life imprisonment with hard labor.

In 1882, the colonial authorities, deeming the presence of the Queens too dangerous on the island, transferred them to Denmark. They were incarcerated in the Women's Prison in Christianshavn, Copenhagen. The sight of these Caribbean women in a European prison was a stark physical manifestation of the colonial relationship. Despite their harsh circumstances, their spirit remained unbroken. Eventually, in 1887, they were returned to St. Croix to serve the remainder of their sentences in Christiansted. Mary Thomas lived out her final years on the island, passing away in 1905.

### Legacy: I Am Queen Mary
For over a century, the story of Queen Mary was kept alive primarily through oral history, folk songs, and the deeply held cultural memory of the Virgin Islands people. She became an icon of resistance, an embodiment of the strength and resilience of Caribbean women.

In recent years, her legacy has received profound international recognition. In 2018, to mark the centennial of the sale of the Danish West Indies to the United States, a monumental public sculpture titled *I Am Queen Mary* was unveiled in Copenhagen. Created collaboratively by Virgin Islands artist La Vaughn Belle and Danish artist Jeannette Ehlers, the striking statue sits in front of the West Indian Warehouse. It depicts Queen Mary seated majestically in a wicker chair—reminiscent of the iconic photograph of Huey P. Newton—holding a torch in one hand and a cane knife in the other.

This monument, Denmark's first public statue of a Black woman, forces a confrontation with the nation's colonial past and honors the heroism of those who fought against it. Queen Mary’s life story—from a laborer in the cane fields to a leader of a massive rebellion, and finally to a global symbol of anti-colonial resistance—demonstrates the profound impact of grassroots activism. She remains a powerful reminder that the fight for labor rights and human dignity in the Caribbean was forged in fire and led by those with the most to lose.b:["$","$L2","c438030d-70b1-49d0-9a4f-076dfce1d681",{"href":"/profiles/queen-mary","className":"group flex flex-col bg-white border border-navy/5 shadow-sm hover:shadow-xl transition-all duration-500","children":[["$","div",null,{"className":"relative aspect-[4/5] overflow-hidden","children":["$","img",null,{"src":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Queen_Mary_Thomas.png","alt":"Queen Mary (Mary Thomas)","className":"object-cover w-full h-full grayscale group-hover:grayscale-0 group-hover:scale-105 transition-all duration-700"}]}],["$","div",null,{"className":"p-6","children":[["$","h3",null,{"className":"font-serif text-xl text-navy mb-2 group-hover:text-gold transition-colors","children":"Queen Mary (Mary Thomas)"}],["$","p",null,{"className":"text-navy/60 text-xs line-clamp-3 leading-relaxed mb-4","children":"$1b"}],"$L1c"]}]]}]
1d:T2b0e,### Introduction

The narrative of Caribbean labor resistance is incomplete without the fiery rebellion of 1878 on the island of St. Croix, Danish West Indies. Known historically as the "Fireburn," this uprising stands as a monumental struggle for human dignity and labor rights in the post-emancipation era. At the absolute vanguard of this rebellion stood a group of women who mobilized, organized, and directed the workers in their demands for fair compensation and basic respect. Among these revered leaders was Mathilda McBean, popularly crowned by her contemporaries and posterity as **Queen Mathilda**. While her life spans the dates of 1849 to 1899 within the institutional records of the [Caribbean Legacy Archive](/profiles/queen-mathilda), her actions in October 1878 carved her name into the history of the Virgin Islands. Alongside [Queen Mary](/profiles/queen-mary) and [Queen Agnes](/profiles/queen-agnes), Queen Mathilda became a symbol of unyielding resistance against colonial exploitation and the oppressive structural remnants of chattel slavery.

### The Post-Emancipation Labor Trap: The 1849 Labor Act

To comprehend the spark that ignited the Fireburn, one must examine the socio-economic reality of St. Croix in the mid-19th century. Although Governor Peter von Scholten had declared the emancipation of all enslaved people in the Danish West Indies in 1848, the colonial planter class and government quickly enacted legislative measures to ensure that the newly freed population remained economically subjugated [1]. The most pernicious of these measures was the Labor Act of 1849 [2].

This Act established a highly restrictive labor system designed to maintain a cheap, stable workforce for the sugar plantations [3]. Under this law, laborers were forced to enter into legally binding, annual contracts. These agreements could only be terminated or changed on a single day of the year: October 1st, commonly referred to as "Contract Day." If a worker failed to secure a new contract or did not wish to renew their existing one, they could be arrested for vagrancy or forced back onto the plantation. Furthermore, the wages were capped at a meager rate—typically between 10 and 15 cents a day—and workers were subjected to harsh disciplinary codes, poor housing, and limited freedom of movement [2]. The physical conditions of labor on the estates differed very little from the pre-1848 era of slavery, fostering a deep, generational resentment among the Afro-Crucian population.

![Historical map showing St. Croix in the Danish West Indies](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4b/St._Croix_in_the_Danish_West_Indies.png)

### The Spark of Frederiksted: October 1, 1878

By the late 1870s, the tension on St. Croix had reached a boiling point [4]. The combination of low wages, a devastating drought, and the arbitrary cruelty of estate managers made the annual Contract Day a focal point of anxiety and resistance. On October 1, 1878, thousands of agricultural laborers gathered in the town of Frederiksted, on the western coast of St. Croix, hoping to negotiate better contracts or find new employers [3].

As the day progressed, rumors spread through the crowd that a popular laborer had been beaten or killed by police. Frustrations quickly boiled over, and the crowd began to clash with the local gendarmerie [4]. When the police retreated into the Frederiksted fort, the laborers took control of the town [1]. What began as a protest rapidly transformed into a full-scale insurrection. The workers dismantled structures, armed themselves, and began setting fire to public buildings, sugar warehouses, and shops. The flames soon spread from Frederiksted into the surrounding countryside, as laborers marched from estate to estate, burning sugarcane fields and great houses. This dramatic, red-lit night gave the uprising its permanent name: the "Fireburn" [5].

### Mathilda McBean: Identity and Early Life

Historical records regarding the early life of Mathilda McBean are scarce, and discrepancies exist between institutional archives and modern historical research. In the official records of the Caribbean Legacy Archive, she is listed as having lived from 1849 to 1899. However, pioneering research by Virgin Islands historians suggests that Mathilda McBean was born around September 1857 at Estate Robe's Hill on St. Croix [6]. This would make her a young woman in her late teens or early twenties—approximately 21 years old—at the time of the 1878 revolt [6].

> "We will not work for these wages; we will burn the country down before we submit."
> — A rallying cry attributed to the leaders of the 1878 Fireburn.

Regardless of the exact year of her birth, Mathilda was a product of the harsh estate labor system. Growing up in the agricultural fields of St. Croix, she witnessed firsthand the transition from chattel slavery to contract servitude. Her youth did not deter her; rather, it provided her with the energy and resolve to challenge the status quo. She possessed a natural eloquence and command that allowed her to sway crowds, making her a natural organizer when the opportunity arose [6].

### Leadership and Mobilization in the Fireburn

During the initial outbreak of the Fireburn in Frederiksted, Mathilda McBean quickly rose to a position of leadership. The laborers organized themselves under "Queens," a title derived from West African traditions of maternal authority and leadership during times of crisis. These Queens served as the operational commanders of the revolt, directing groups of workers, coordinating the movement of people across the island, and providing the ideological and emotional support necessary to sustain the rebellion [1].

Queen Mathilda was particularly noted for her role as a primary mobilizer. While [Queen Mary](/profiles/queen-mary) was known for her fierce, confrontational stance at the forefront of physical confrontations, and [Queen Agnes](/profiles/queen-agnes) organized the logistical transport of fuel and supplies, Queen Mathilda focused on the critical task of mass communication and recruitment. She traversed the estates, urging workers to leave their fields, refuse their contracts, and join the march [1]. She was instrumental in organizing the collection of kerosene and the preparation of torches, which were used to set fire to the sugar estates [6]. Witnesses during her subsequent trial testified that Mathilda was seen leading large groups of chanting laborers, holding a torch aloft, and calling for the destruction of the plantations that had enslaved them. Over the course of several days, the rebels burned over 50 plantations and devastated the colonial economy of St. Croix [4].

![Map of St. Croix during the Danish colonial era](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e0/Map_of_St._Croix_Danish_West_Indies.jpg)

### Arrest, Trial, and Exile in Denmark

The Danish colonial government responded to the Fireburn with brutal military force. Troops were dispatched, and martial law was declared. Over the course of the next few weeks, the rebellion was systematically suppressed. Hundreds of laborers were arrested, and dozens were summarily executed by firing squad.

Mathilda McBean, along with the other primary Queens, was arrested in late October 1878 [4]. The colonial authorities, recognizing the deep influence of these women, conducted extensive trials to determine the ringleaders of the revolt. The trials revealed the highly organized nature of the uprising and the central role played by the Queens. Mathilda and her co-conspirators were originally sentenced to death for their participation in the rebellion and arson [6]. However, the Danish Crown, wary of creating martyrs and facing international scrutiny, commuted the death sentences to life imprisonment with hard labor [1].

In 1882, Queen Mathilda, [Queen Mary](/profiles/queen-mary), and [Queen Agnes](/profiles/queen-agnes) were extradited to Denmark to serve their sentences [3]. They were incarcerated in the Christianshavn Women's Prison (*Kvindefængslet*) in Copenhagen [1]. The transition from the tropical climate of St. Croix to the damp, freezing cells of Copenhagen was incredibly harsh [6]. Despite the physical toll, historical records from the prison note that the Crucian women maintained a dignified and resilient demeanor, refusing to be broken by their captors.

### Return and Final Years

In the late 1880s, facing growing public pressure in Denmark and persistent unrest in the Virgin Islands, the Danish government decided to commute the sentences of the surviving Fireburn leaders. In 1889, Queen Mathilda, along with [Queen Mary](/profiles/queen-mary) and [Queen Agnes](/profiles/queen-agnes), was allowed to return to St. Croix [3].

Upon their return, they were met as heroes by the local population. However, the colonial authorities kept them under close surveillance, restricting their movement and preventing them from participating in any further labor organizing [1]. Mathilda McBean spent her remaining years in relative obscurity, working in agricultural labor but revered by her community as a living legend of the struggle for freedom. She passed away around 1899, marking the end of a life dedicated to the fight against colonial oppression.

### Legacy and Commemoration

The legacy of Queen Mathilda and the Fireburn remains a cornerstone of the cultural identity of the U.S. Virgin Islands. In the decades following the revolt, the story of the Queens was kept alive through oral traditions, folk songs, and annual commemorations on Contract Day (October 1st).

In the 20th century, as the Virgin Islands witnessed the rise of modern civil rights leaders like [David Hamilton Jackson](/profiles/hamilton-jackson), the Fireburn was recognized as the foundational event in the island's labor movement. Modern political and civic leaders, including Governors [Alexander Farrelly](/profiles/alexander-farrelly) and [Cyril E. King](/profiles/cyril-king), have repeatedly highlighted the historical debt the territory owes to the 1878 rebels. Furthermore, cultural figures such as the musician [Alton Augustus Adams](/profiles/alton-adams) drew inspiration from the spirit of resistance that these Queens embodied. The "Three Queens Fountain," a bronze monument located at Blackbeard's Castle in Charlotte Amalie, St. Thomas, stands as a permanent tribute to Queen Mathilda, [Queen Mary](/profiles/queen-mary), and [Queen Agnes](/profiles/queen-agnes) [7]. In recent years, the collaborative monument *I Am Queen Mary*, created by artists La Vaughn Belle and Jeannette Ehlers in Copenhagen, has further elevated the global recognition of these women, connecting the history of St. Croix to the broader dialogue on Danish colonial legacy and the African diaspora. Queen Mathilda's life serves as an enduring reminder that the fight for labor rights and human dignity is often led by the most marginalized, whose courage can shake the foundations of colonial power.c:["$","$L2","6308fdf3-8818-4403-8edd-05c62e91e809",{"href":"/profiles/queen-mathilda","className":"group flex flex-col bg-white border border-navy/5 shadow-sm hover:shadow-xl transition-all duration-500","children":[["$","div",null,{"className":"relative aspect-[4/5] overflow-hidden","children":["$","img",null,{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Luxembourg_-_La_Reine_Mathilde.jpg/960px-Luxembourg_-_La_Reine_Mathilde.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail","alt":"Queen Mathilda","className":"object-cover w-full h-full grayscale group-hover:grayscale-0 group-hover:scale-105 transition-all duration-700"}]}],["$","div",null,{"className":"p-6","children":[["$","h3",null,{"className":"font-serif text-xl text-navy mb-2 group-hover:text-gold transition-colors","children":"Queen Mathilda"}],["$","p",null,{"className":"text-navy/60 text-xs line-clamp-3 leading-relaxed mb-4","children":"$1d"}],"$L1e"]}]]}]
1f:T2eb3,# Rothschild Francis: The Unyielding Voice of the Virgin Islands

Rothschild "Polly" Francis (1891–1963) stands as a towering, transformative figure in the history of the United States Virgin Islands. A pioneering labor leader, self-educated intellectual, fierce civil rights activist, and fearless journalist, Francis defined the early struggle for democracy and civil liberties in the territory following its transfer from Danish to American sovereignty in 1917. At a time when the local population faced significant economic hardship, systemic disenfranchisement, and strict military rule, Francis emerged as a relentless advocate for the marginalized and oppressed. He is best remembered for founding the influential newspaper *The Emancipator*, fiercely campaigning for a civilian government to replace the U.S. Naval administration, and demanding full United States citizenship for all Virgin Islanders. Through his unyielding dedication to democratic ideals, he fundamentally altered the political landscape of the Caribbean.

### Early Life in the Danish West Indies

Rothschild Francis was born in 1891 on the island of St. Thomas, which was then a crucial part of the Danish West Indies. Growing up during the final decades of Danish colonial rule, Francis witnessed firsthand the vast inequalities that defined Caribbean society of the era. The local economy, which had historically been driven by the brutal realities of the trans-Atlantic slave trade, sugar cultivation, and maritime commerce, had long been in a state of severe decline. The majority of the Afro-Caribbean population suffered under systemic poverty, agonizingly low wages, and severely limited educational opportunities. Social mobility was virtually non-existent for those outside the privileged colonial elite.

Despite the lack of formal educational structures for the working class, Francis was a man of immense intellectual curiosity. Primarily self-educated, he possessed a voracious appetite for knowledge, studying history, law, and political philosophy. This self-directed education cultivated within him an acute sense of justice and a deep understanding of the mechanics of oppression—insights that would guide his lifelong crusade for equality.

In 1917, amidst the geopolitical anxieties of World War I, the United States purchased the islands from Denmark for $25 million, renaming them the United States Virgin Islands. For many local residents, the transfer of sovereignty brought a profound wave of optimism. They firmly believed that becoming part of the United States—a nation fundamentally founded on principles of liberty and justice—would usher in an era of democratic ideals, economic prosperity, and the immediate granting of American citizenship.

However, the reality of the transfer fell drastically short of these lofty expectations. Rather than integrating the islands as a democratic territory, the U.S. government placed them under the jurisdiction of the Department of the Navy. Rather than experiencing the promises of democracy, Virgin Islanders found themselves subjected to strict, autocratic military rule. They were governed by naval officers who possessed virtually unchecked executive, legislative, and judicial powers. The local population remained devoid of constitutional protections, political self-determination, and the U.S. citizenship they so deeply coveted. It was within this crucible of profound disappointment and paternalistic colonial administration that Rothschild Francis forged his powerful political ideology.

> "The transfer of the Virgin Islands did not bring the freedom and democracy promised by the American flag; instead, it brought military rule. We demanded nothing less than our birthright as citizens—a fight that could not be silenced by the gavel of a naval judge."

### *The Emancipator* and the Power of the Press

Recognizing that the people desperately needed a platform to voice their grievances and organize their resistance, Francis turned to the power of journalism. In 1921, he founded a newspaper aptly named *The Emancipator*. Through its pages, Francis launched a sustained, courageous, and highly effective campaign against the abuses and systemic failures of the naval administration. *The Emancipator* was not merely a newspaper; it served as the intellectual, social, and political heart of the Virgin Islands' early civil rights movement.

Francis used the publication to ruthlessly expose government corruption, criticize the heavy-handed and often arbitrary policies of naval officials, and highlight the severe economic exploitation of the working class. He consistently fought for fair wages, better working conditions, and the fundamental right of local residents to have a meaningful say in their own governance. By articulating the deepest frustrations of the common people, Francis quickly became the most visible and vocal opponent of naval rule in the territory.

His editorials were sharp, uncompromising, and deeply rooted in the democratic principles espoused by the United States Constitution—principles he argued were being hypocritically denied to the people of the Virgin Islands. He drew stark contrasts between the democratic rhetoric of the American mainland and the dictatorial reality of the islands' governance, creating a compelling moral argument that resonated both locally and abroad.

![Rothschild Francis Square in Charlotte Amalie](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ea/Market_Square%2C_Charlotte_Amalie.jpg)

### The Fight for Civilian Government and Citizenship

Francis’s activism was by no means confined to the printing press. He was fundamentally a man of action who took the fight directly to the halls of political power. As an elected member of the Colonial Council, the local legislative body at the time, he pushed tirelessly for legislative reforms and relentlessly challenged the colonial authority of the naval governors at every turn.

His political vision was clear and uncompromising: the complete removal of military rule, the establishment of a fully functional civilian government, and the extension of full United States citizenship to all Virgin Islanders. To achieve these ambitious goals, Francis realized he needed to build power from the ground up. He organized labor unions to empower the working class, leading strikes and negotiations that demanded basic dignity and a living wage for laborers who had long been exploited.

Simultaneously, Francis built strategic alliances with prominent progressive organizations on the U.S. mainland. He collaborated extensively with the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), utilizing their legal expertise and political connections to amplify his cause. Francis traveled to Washington, D.C., to testify directly before the United States Congress. During these landmark hearings, he passionately and eloquently articulated the plight of his people. He exposed the inherent contradictions of a purportedly democratic nation administering a colonial military regime, forcing American lawmakers to confront the realities of their territorial policies.

His tireless efforts laid the critical groundwork that would eventually lead to the granting of U.S. citizenship to Virgin Islanders in 1927 (which was later expanded in 1932), as well as the transition to a civilian government under the Department of the Interior in 1931. Although these sweeping victories took time to fully materialize, it was unequivocally Francis’s early, uncompromising agitation that set the wheels of historical change in motion.

### Persecution, Legal Battles, and Resilience

Unsurprisingly, Francis’s relentless challenge to the status quo made him a prime target for the naval administration. The military governors and their appointed officials viewed him not as a legitimate civil rights leader, but as a dangerous agitator, a subversive threat to public order, and an enemy of the state. As a result, Francis faced intense political persecution and a series of exhausting legal battles designed specifically to silence him, discredit his movement, and bankrupt his newspaper.

In 1924, he was convicted of criminal libel after publishing an editorial that heavily criticized a local police officer for brutality and abuse of power. The naval-appointed judges, who operated without the standard checks and balances of a civilian justice system, were eager to penalize him. Despite aggressively appealing the decision and receiving significant legal support and representation from the ACLU, the conviction was ultimately upheld.

Just two years later, in 1926, the administration struck again. Francis was indicted and convicted on charges of embezzlement. Modern historians, legal scholars, and contemporary Virgin Islands legislators have heavily scrutinized these convictions, almost universally characterizing them as deeply suspicious, entirely politically motivated, and orchestrated specifically to crush his political influence and destroy his reputation among the masses.

These drawn-out legal battles exacted a heavy toll on Francis, both personally and financially. The relentless harassment, combined with the financial ruin brought upon *The Emancipator*, eventually forced him to step away from the forefront of Virgin Islands politics. He subsequently relocated to the U.S. mainland, where he lived out the remainder of his life in relative obscurity. However, his spirit remained unbroken, and the ideological seeds he had planted in the minds of Virgin Islanders continued to grow and bear fruit long after his departure.

### Legacy and Modern Recognition

Rothschild Francis passed away in 1963, living just long enough to see many of his core political goals realized, though he rarely received the credit he deserved during his lifetime. Today, his legacy as a foundational figure in the Virgin Islands' quest for civil rights remains deeply ingrained in the territory's historical consciousness. He is revered not just as a labor leader or a journalist, but as a profound visionary who sacrificed his own freedom, reputation, and livelihood to secure the democratic rights of future generations.

His extraordinary contributions have been memorialized in numerous ways across the Virgin Islands, ensuring that his name will never be forgotten. The historic Market Square in Charlotte Amalie, St. Thomas—a central commercial and social gathering place for the community for centuries—was officially renamed Rothschild Francis Square in his honor. This bustling center of commerce now serves as a permanent monument to his fight for the working class.

In Educators Park on St. Thomas, a prominent bust of Francis stands proudly alongside other revered historical figures such as [Edith Williams](/profiles/edith-williams) and [J. Antonio Jarvis](/profiles/j-antonio-jarvis). October 5th is officially designated as Rothschild Francis Day in the territory, a day dedicated to reflecting on his immense contributions to civil liberties, journalism, and labor rights.

Furthermore, in recent years, the Virgin Islands Legislature has undertaken significant efforts to posthumously pardon Francis for his libel and embezzlement convictions, formally recognizing the unjust, corrupt, and politically motivated nature of his prosecution by the naval administration. This movement for exoneration reflects a broader, crucial reckoning with the colonial history of the territory and serves as the ultimate vindication of a man who was always on the right side of history.

Rothschild Francis’s life is a powerful testament to the enduring power of the press, the unbreakable resilience of the human spirit, and the perpetual quest for equality. He boldly dared to demand that the promises of democracy be extended across the ocean to the shores of the Virgin Islands, and in doing so, he forever altered the political and social trajectory of his homeland.d:["$","$L2","1b53f65f-4bf8-4f11-adc9-2f90e6e140a3",{"href":"/profiles/rothschild-francis","className":"group flex flex-col bg-white border border-navy/5 shadow-sm hover:shadow-xl transition-all duration-500","children":[["$","div",null,{"className":"relative aspect-[4/5] overflow-hidden","children":["$","img",null,{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5c/Rothschild_Francis.png","alt":"Rothschild Francis","className":"object-cover w-full h-full grayscale group-hover:grayscale-0 group-hover:scale-105 transition-all duration-700"}]}],["$","div",null,{"className":"p-6","children":[["$","h3",null,{"className":"font-serif text-xl text-navy mb-2 group-hover:text-gold transition-colors","children":"Rothschild Francis"}],["$","p",null,{"className":"text-navy/60 text-xs line-clamp-3 leading-relaxed mb-4","children":"$1f"}],"$L20"]}]]}]
